summary.summary: Lancashire ended 2025/26 with £948.8m of borrowing (down £98.8m, with maturing debt partly replaced by internal borrowing) and £531.7m of investments, but around 60% of its debt now matures within 12 months — nearly double its own one-third aim — after it deliberately stayed short while long-term rates spiked following the war in Iran. Rather than pay roughly £1.2m extra to extend the debt, it is asking Full Council to raise the under-12-month maturity limit from 50% to 75%, cut all lower maturity limits to 0%, and adopt a departure from the CIPFA Code's maturity measurement convention. The treasury budget overspent by £2.7m in-year (investment returns below budget plus extra working-capital borrowing to finance the schools-grant deficit), covered from an earmarked reserve, and its Very Long-Term Investment Portfolio remains worth significantly less than was paid for it, with no figures disclosed in this report.
summary.as_of_doc: Treasury Management Strategy Update and 2025/26 Outturn

signals.headline: c.60% of £948.8m debt matures within 12 months at 31 March 2026, against a one-third aim; the under-12-month upper limit is proposed to rise from 50% to 75% for 2026/27 with all lower limits cut to 0%
signals.why: Well over half the debt book must be rolled over inside a year at elevated short rates, and the council is loosening its own guardrail rather than paying c.£1.2m more to term the debt out.

signals.headline: 2025/26 treasury budget overspent by £2.7m, driven partly by increased borrowing for working capital to finance DSG overspending; met from an earmarked reserve
signals.why: The schools-funding deficit is already translating into extra borrowing need and treasury cost, a pressure the council says is now built into current-year budgets.

signals.headline: Asking Full Council to raise the under-12-month maturity limit from 50% to 75% and depart from the CIPFA Code convention (c.60% of £948.8m already short)
signals.why: Raising the limit to fit the position, rather than the position to fit the limit, shifts refinancing risk onto future rate conditions.

news_drafts.headline: Lancashire County Council cut its borrowing by £98.8m to £948.8m in 2025/26, using its own cash
news_drafts.lead:
Lancashire County Council reduced its total borrowing by £98.8m during 2025/26, from £1,047.6m to £948.8m, according to the treasury management report (the account of how the council borrows and invests its spare cash) before Full Council on 15 October 2026.

The report says the fall was "due to maturing debt being partly replaced by internal borrowing". Internal borrowing means using the council's own cash to pay for long-lived assets such as buildings and roads instead of taking out a new loan. That saves interest, but it uses up cash the council would otherwise hold. Rather than keep separate investment holdings, the council used available cash to reduce how much it needed to borrow.

The papers give the average interest rate the council achieved over the year as 4.00%. The benchmark it is measured against, SONIA (the Sterling Overnight Index Average, a standard measure of short-term sterling interest rates), stood at 4.01%. The council's rate therefore tracked the benchmark closely, a hundredth of a percentage point below it.

news_drafts.headline: Lancashire cuts employer pension contributions to third-lowest nationally
news_drafts.lead: Lancashire has cut employer contribution rates to the pension fund from 17.1% to 9.1% following its 2025 valuation, which will materially reduce the council's annual pension costs going forward. The new rate is the third-lowest among 86 Local Government Pension Scheme funds in England and Wales. The Fund achieved this through a healthy funding level of 132%, meaning its assets exceed the liabilities owed to members. The funding level has fallen by two percentage points from 134% a year ago, and the Committee is monitoring the trend.
news_drafts.paper_title: Lancashire County Pension Fund Annual Report 2025/26

findings.headline: Local investment allocation target increased from 1.2% to 3% of fund assets
findings.detail: The Fund is revising its local investment objective to increase the target allocation from approximately £130m (1.2%) to £420m (3%) of total fund assets over the medium to long term, with a maximum of 4%. The expanded target focuses on job creation, skills development, infrastructure and affordable housing within Lancashire.
findings.matters: Represents a material strategic shift in capital deployment; peers and lenders would track this as evidence of the fund's approach to balancing investment returns with local economic development priorities.
findings.quote: The administering authority aims to increase its allocation to local investment opportunities from £130m (c 1.2%) to 3% (c.£420m) of total Fund assets over the medium to long term and may not exceed 4% of the total portfolio.

findings.headline: Pension fund funded at 134% at 2025 valuation
findings.detail: The Fund's Funding Level at the 2025 valuation was 134%, substantially ahead of the Risk Appetite Statement target of maintaining above 125% in the short to medium term. This surplus position indicates the fund has sufficient assets to meet its pension liabilities with a significant buffer, reducing near-term pressure for employer contribution increases.
findings.matters: For the council and its lenders, a well-funded pension scheme reduces the risk of future contribution rate rises that would impact the council's budget and borrowing needs.
findings.figures: Funding level 134% at 2025 valuation; RAS target above 125%
findings.quote: At the 2025 valuation, the Fund's Funding Level was 134%.

findings.headline: Local investment target increased from £150m (1.2% of portfolio) to 3% (approximately £400m), with permission to accept lower returns for social and economic benefits
findings.detail: The Fund will increase its local investment target from £150m (1.2% of portfolio) to approximately £400m (3% of portfolio) with a tolerance range of 0-4%. The policy permits the Fund to accept concessions on risk or return where an investment delivers enhanced social and economic benefits to Lancashire. 'Local' is defined as Lancashire's geographical footprint with flexibility for opportunities marginally outside the county.
findings.matters: This represents a significant capital redeployment (£250m additional) and signals a policy shift to accept below-market returns for social benefit, which raises questions about fiduciary duty and could affect the fund's ability to meet contribution obligations.
findings.figures: Current target £150m (1.2% of portfolio); proposed target 3% (approximately £400m); tolerance range 0-4%
findings.quote: Where an investment is considered to deliver an enhanced level of social and economic benefits to Lancashire, the Fund will permit a concession to risk or return considerations.

findings.headline: Strategic Asset Allocation revised: Global Equities 43.5% to 45.0%, Private Credit 9.0% to 7.5%, Liquid Credit 15.0% to 12.5%, UK Government Bonds 0.0% to 2.5%
findings.detail: The Pension Fund Committee approved a revised Strategic Asset Allocation designed to balance long-term affordability and stability of employer contribution rates. Changes include a 1.5 percentage point increase in Global Equities, reductions in both Private and Liquid Credit exposures, and introduction of a new 2.5% allocation to UK Government Bonds. The revised SAA will replace the current allocation in the final ISS.
findings.matters: Pension fund asset allocation directly determines the investment returns and risk profile that underpin future employer contribution rates; changes that adjust expected returns or volatility have material implications for council budgets.
findings.figures: Global Equities 43.5% to 45.0%; Private Credit 9.0% to 7.5%; Liquid Credit 15.0% to 12.5%; UK Government Bonds 0.0% to 2.5%
findings.quote: Having considered feedback from the Committee, and working with the Investment Panel, LPPI produced a proposed SAA for the Fund. This was based on the view of Committee members that the strategy should aim to balance long term affordability of employer contribution rates with stability of these rates.

findings.headline: Pension administration improvement work paused due to resource demands of SCAPE discount rate changes and Access & Fairness regulatory reforms
findings.detail: The council has suspended non-urgent improvement projects across pension administration because staff have been redeployed to manage the SCAPE discount rate changes and new Access & Fairness/Access & Protection regulatory requirements. This signals sustained resource pressure on the pension administration function.
findings.matters: A lender assesses operational resilience; pausing improvement work indicates resource constraints and suggests the pension administration team faces sustained operational strain.
findings.quote: Work on other improvement activities has been paused due to SCAPE and Access & Fairness and Access & Protection regulatory changes.
